item.title: King-Hinds wins reelection in landslide; Governor, AG races head to runoff
item.description: Republican incumbent Kimberlyn King-Hinds won reelection Tuesday as the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands' delegate to the U.S. House of Representatives, capturing nearly two-thirds of the vote in a decisive victory that highlighted the 2026 general election. item.content:encoded:
Republican incumbent Kimberlyn King-Hinds won reelection Tuesday as the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands' delegate to the U.S. House of Representatives, capturing nearly two-thirds of the vote in a decisive victory that highlighted the 2026 general election.

Unofficial results showed King-Hinds receiving 8,194 votes, or 63.7% of ballots cast in the delegate race, securing another two-year term in Congress. Independent challenger Galvin Sablan Deleon Guerrero garnered 4,675 votes, or 36%.

While the delegate race produced a clear winner, voters left the contests for governor and attorney general unsettled, triggering runoff elections under CNMI law.

The Republican gubernatorial ticket of Ralph DLG Torres and Benjamin Jones Jr. finished first but failed to capture a majority of votes cast. They will face the independent team of Blas Jonathan Attao and Edmund S. Villagomez in a runoff election.

The independent ticket of Lawrence Camacho and Edith E. Deleon Guerrero finished third and was eliminated from contention.

In the attorney general race, attorneys Joaquin DLG Torres and Michael Evangelista advanced to a runoff after neither candidate secured more than 50% of the vote. Attorney Jonathan Robert Glass Jr. placed third.

The race for attorney general was among the night's closest contests. Evangelista edged Glass by only 18 votes to claim the second runoff spot and keep his campaign alive.

Under CNMI law, a runoff election is required when no gubernatorial ticket or attorney general candidate receives more than half of all votes cast and counted in the general election. The runoff must be held within 14 days after the Commonwealth Election Commission certifies the election results.

Voters also considered whether to convene a constitutional convention to propose amendments to the CNMI Constitution. The proposal received majority support, with 7,602 voters casting ballots in favor and 4,324 voting against.

However, the measure failed because it did not meet the constitutional requirement that at least two-thirds of all votes cast on the question commonwealthwide be in favor. As a result, no constitutional convention will be convened.

The results set up two weeks of campaigning before voters return to the polls to decide the governor's office and attorney general post, while King-Hinds prepares to serve another term as the CNMI's representative in Washington.

item.title: Ada/Calvo win Adelup; Limtiaco new delegate; Tydingco wins AG race; Republican majority in Legislature
item.description: Republicans Tony Ada and E.J. Calvo were elected as the new governor and lieutenant governor of Guam on Tuesday. Democrat Alicia Limtiaco defeated incumbent Republican Del. James Moylan in the race for Congress.
item.content:encoded:
Republicans Tony Ada and E.J. Calvo were elected as the new governor and lieutenant governor of Guam on Tuesday.

Democrat Alicia Limtiaco defeated incumbent Republican Del. James Moylan in the race for Congress.

Phillip Tydingco beat incumbent Doug Moylan in the race for attorney general.

In the legislative race, Republicans took the majority of seats, with eight to the seven held by Democrats.

Legislative winners were: Chris Barnett (i) (DEM) Amanda Shelton (DEM) Sabrina Salas Matanane (i) (REP) Jesse Lujan (i) (REP) Chris Duenas (i) (REP) Telena Nelson (DEM) Telo Taitague (i) (REP) Hoa Van Nguyen (REP) William Parkinson (i) (DEM) Donna Quinata (DEM) Clynt Ridgell (DEM) Vince Borja (i) (REP) Shelly Calvo (i) (REP) Kallen Perez (DEM) Eulogio Shawn Gumataotao (i) (REP)

item.title: Connecticut bakers are bringing joy back to election day, one cake at a time
item.description: Election day can be described in many ways: stressful, overwhelming, anxiety-inducing — and the list goes on. But in Hartford, Connecticut, it's a piece of cake — specifically a mutli-tiered red, white and blue patriotic cake decorated with an American flag, stars and a bald eagle made entirely of frosting.
item.content:encoded:
Election day can be described in many ways: stressful, overwhelming, anxiety-inducing — and the list goes on.

But in Hartford, Connecticut, it's a piece of cake — specifically a mutli-tiered red, white and blue patriotic cake decorated with an American flag, stars and a bald eagle made entirely of frosting.

This masterpiece won the annual Election Cake Bake-Off at Connecticut's Old State House in Harford, CT. Nicole Sousa, the events and outreach manager at the Old State House, told Morning Edition about the Bake Off and rich tradition behind it.

Election cake first appeared in Hartford, in 1771, when the northeast United States was still a collection of 13 original colonies. Connecticut was a pioneer in early self-government, and it was one of the only regions who could elect their own officials.

"It was definitely something that Connecticut, as a colony and then later as a state, celebrated and really felt attached to," Sousa said.

So, election day was joyous. It was marked with parties, parades and community-wide celebrations — often involving cake.

But election cakes looked nothing like they do now. At that time, the iconic cakes resembled a tough, fruit cake, often soaked in alcohol.

Plus, this cake definitely couldn't fit in your modern fridge. In the eighteenth century, Sousa said the cakes were made using 30 quarts of flour, ten pounds of butter, 14 pounds of sugar, 12 pounds of raisins, three dozen eggs and over a quart of wine or brandy. Sousa said the massive cakes were baked to feed huge crowds of celebrating voters.

Writer Amelia Simmons featured a scaled-down recipe for traditional election cake in American Cookery , which is widely recognized as the first American cookbook.

More than 250 years later, Connecticut's Old State House hosted its fifth annual Election Cake Bake Off on Oct. 26. Professional pastry chefs and bakers were challenged to create a deliciously non-partisan, election-themed cake that inspires voters and celebrates American democracy.

"They're in it to win it for sure," Sousa said. "But they're also in it for the love of Election Day, the love of baking and the love of the idea of election cakes."

A panel of judges scored the cakes based on presentation, creativity and of course taste. The winning confection was crowned the official Connecticut Election Cake of 2026, and its baker received a commission to make Connecticut's Old State House birthday cake in 2027.

This year's winner was a mother-daughter duo led by Sophia Grestini of Amy's Cakes LLC in Cheshire, CT.

Their cake had four layers, alternating between sweet lemon blueberry and traditional spiced sponge flavors. The exterior was covered in red, white, blue and gold accents and featured iconic election day symbols like an "I voted" pin, ballot box and American flag.

On the second tier, handcrafted fondant figures of a donkey and elephant represented the two major political parties. Perched atop the masterpiece was a bald eagle sculpted entirely from frosting — guarding the cake from danger, or at least wandering forks.

Sousa said the cake was delicious, but, most importantly, the bakers had fun making it. She called the event joyous.

"That's what we're trying to do with the election cake contest — we're trying to bring that joy back to Election Day," Sousa said. "It should be fun, it should be a way to show that you're contributing to your country and part of your community."

item.title: Supreme Court leans toward LGBTQ exclusion for publicly funded Catholic preschools

item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court's conservative majority seemed inclined Tuesday to rule that the four-year-old children of gay and trans parents can be barred from a state-funded pre-K program.

In 2022, Colorado adopted a state-wide program to provide all four-year-olds with an early education. The program, paid for by the taxpayers to the tune of $6,300 per child per year, was open to all, including religious groups. The only caveat was that the preschool program had to comply with the state law barring discrimination based on race, religion, ethnicity, or other categories.

Although the Catholic Church initially supported the program, and the nonprofit Catholic Charities still participates in it, the Denver archdiocese maintained that compliance with the state's nondiscrimination mandate violates the Constitution's guarantee to the free exercise of religion.

The Denver archdiocese — though not all others in the state — wants an exemption from the law so that it can obtain state funding while at the same time barring from its program the children of gay and trans parents.

The conservative justices on Tuesday seemed likely to oblige their request. Justice Neil Gorsuch angrily suggested that Colorado was deliberately defying an earlier series of decisions , inquiring whether "we were just wasting our time for the last ten years on those cases."

And Justice Amy Coney Barrett seemed to question the state's good faith. "It's hard to imagine that Colorado couldn't have seen this coming," she opined.

Justice Brett Kavanaugh agreed, referring to Colorado's law as a provocation.

"Why not seek the win-win," he asked. "There are 2,000 schools. There are only 34 Catholic schools. There are plenty of opportunities to respect the rights of the religious believers and respect the ability of LGBT parents to find among the 2,000 schools [an] appropriate fit for their children."

Justice Samuel Alito followed up, contending that "we have little evidence of a practical problem. Little evidence, if any evidence…that there are LGBTQ couples who cannot find other preschools to send their children to."

But Colorado Deputy Solicitor General Helen Norton pointed to the specific case of a rejected student, and disputed assertions that these schools are easily interchangeable.

"Think of the parent who needs a school that opens at 7 a.m. so she can get the bus that takes her to work. Think of the parent who needs a school that will take all three of her kids, so she doesn't have to shuttle them among three different schools," she said.

The court's three liberal justices signaled strong disagreement with the conservatives.

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson put her views this way: "There's no principled basis, I think, to distinguish between an entity that says, 'My religious faith says my children can't go to school with the children of gay people,' from a religious entity that says, 'my religion says my children can't go to school with the children of Black people.'"

Justice Elena Kagan, barely suppressing her sarcasm, added that, "Even though religious people are being treated the same way on the face of the statute, that's not enough. They need a special accommodation. They need to be treated differently from other people."

And Justice Sonia Sotomayor directly challenged the lawyer for the archdiocese, Nicholas R. Reaves.

"Bottom line is your school can reject a child because their parents are homosexual," she addressed him.

Of the court's conservatives, only Chief Justice John Roberts expressed any skepticism at all about the archdiocese's argument.

All six of the court's conservatives were raised Catholic. So too was liberal Justice Sotomayor.

A decision in the case is expected by summer 2027.

item.title: A Binance engineer thought he was interviewing for a job. Then the hackers pounced
item.description: The massive $6.3 billion cyber heist suffered by crypto exchange Binance last week may have taken place in only about twenty minutes — but the attacks were months in the making. That's according an initial assessment released by Binance on Tuesday about how it suffered the world's biggest-ever cyber heist by hackers the FBI has identified as being a North Korean state-sponsored unit.
item.content:encoded:
The massive $6.3 billion cyber heist suffered by crypto exchange Binance last week may have taken place in only about twenty minutes — but the attacks were months in the making.

That's according an initial assessment released by Binance on Tuesday about how it suffered the world's biggest-ever cyber heist by hackers the FBI has identified as being a North Korean state-sponsored unit.

Those findings show the hackers first tried testing and penetrating Binance's security systems back in June, though the crypto exchange was able to detect that attempt and stop it.

Though unsuccessful, that attempt allowed the hackers — identified by the FBI as a North Korean military unit called TraderTraitor — to learn more about Binance and its systems.

Then, the hackers tried again. In September, a Binance engineer was contacted in a job-hunting platform by a person posing as a "project director" from a company that turned out to be fictious.

The engineer then conducted a first-round interview with a supposed HR representative from the fake company. The hackers used this interview to "build trust," with the Binance employee, the exchange said. The interviewer even shared supposed social media accounts, as well as personal photos and videos with the Binance engineer.

"This was more advanced and deceptive than previously seen social engineering approaches," Binance said in its assessment.

The engineer was then told he would be conducting a second interview with the supposed CEO of the company in a popular social chat app. It was in this interview that the Binance employee — who was at his work laptop — was asked to download "an assignment" as part of the job recruitment process.

Instead, the "assignment" contained malicious code that allowed hackers to build out an attack that culminated last week when hackers made off with over $6 billion worth of crypto currencies held by Binance's customers at the exchange.

Binance said in the statement posted on X that the company is taking a series of actions, including an independent cybersecurity review to prevent future attacks. On Monday the exchange had said it had already replaced most of the stolen crypto currencies stolen by customers using its own funds.

"This should not have happened," Binance said in its assessment on Tuesday. "And we apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry."

item.title: For Ukraine's Kherson region, a short ceasefire meant a momentary return to normal life
item.description: KHERSON, Ukraine — In this city where Russian drones usually fill the skies, Olena Soboleva could not easily walk down the street to meet her best friend, Anna Herasimenko. Then came last week's truce, negotiated by First Lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV, in a corner of southern Ukraine that included Kherson.
item.content:encoded:
KHERSON, Ukraine — In this city where Russian drones usually fill the skies, Olena Soboleva could not easily walk down the street to meet her best friend, Anna Herasimenko.

Then came last week's truce, negotiated by First Lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV, in a corner of southern Ukraine that included Kherson.

This weekend, the two friends, both 21, took the opportunity to venture outside to autumnal skies clear of drones and guided bombs.

"No drones, no explosions," Soboleva says. "No one wants to kill you."

They passed families strolling with their kids, shoppers stocking up on supplies and couples holding hands. They lined up at a cafe filled with paintings of cats.

"The city seems alive," says Herasimenko, "just like it used to be."

Over the weekend, she had also ventured to a salon.

"I did my nails," she says, showing off fresh burgundy polish. "The streets are full of people, just as they were in the past."

The truce ended Sunday night. Russia and Ukraine agreed to it in order to help Oleshky, a town across the Dnipro River from Kherson. Russian troops occupied Oleshky in 2022 and mined the land around it. Food and medicine rarely got through. NPR spoke to the families of residents there, who said their loved ones survived on pickles and boiled weeds.

Over the weekend, hundreds of Oleshky residents were evacuated, eventually escorted into northern Ukraine on buses. Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's ombudsman — the country's independent watchdog for human rights — thanked Melania Trump for ensuring that the ceasefire, which lasted from Oct. 27 to Nov. 1, happened.

"I believe they can be upheld and honored," Lubinets said about truces between Ukraine and Russia.

Even a short pause in hostilities was a respite for Kherson. Russian troops occupied the city for several months in 2022, until local partisans spied for Ukrainian soldiers, who then forced the Russians out of the city.

Since 2024, Russian troops based across the river have hunted Kherson residents with FPV (first-person-view) drones strapped with explosives. The highway into Kherson is shrouded in tunnels of heavy mesh nets to protect locals from these drones. These anti-drone nets also cover Kherson's streets and many of its buildings.

This weekend, cars pulled up next to the Greek-style monument marking the city's gateway.

Svitlana Vorobiova, a retired police officer, drove here from a safer city where she now lives. She took photos with her children at the monument.

"I have a place in Kherson, and my parents are also here," she says, and her voice breaks. Tears fill her eyes.

"I brought my son with me," Vorobiova says. "He hasn't been here in four years. He said, 'I cannot believe I'm in my hometown!'"

Inside the city, Volodymyr Mykolaienko, a former mayor of Kherson, strolls past the crushed remains of a once-grand administrative building. Locals stop him and shake his hand. He says he's happy to see so many people outside.

"I walk around the city a lot these days," he says. "I cannot sit still at home."

Mykolaienko, 66, spent years as a prisoner of war in Russia, confined to tiny rooms, starved and tortured. Russian troops arrested him in Kherson in early 2022, when the city was under Russian occupation. Mykolaienko was freed last year in a prisoner exchange and returned to Kherson, where his family still lives.

This truce allowed him to visit his father's grave. The cemetery is in a part of the city that's usually filled with drones.

"I could not hold myself back," he says. "I was able to do exactly what I have long wanted to do — to talk to my father, pray, thank him for my life and to tell him what was happening to our city."

At a busy bus stop, oncology nurse Olena Yehorova smiles at a gray-haired man playing folk music on his accordion.

"This truce has been such a relief," she says. "The people in our city have been able to breathe. Of course, we still walk around with caution, because you cannot trust the Russians."

She couldn't help looking up at the sky. A few hours later, the truce was over. She said she expects new attacks to resume at any time.

NPR's Polina Lytvynova contributed to this report from Kyiv.
